quotes.note: Sustained external narration reports the character's actions and inner distress without a participating narrator.
Extended narration identifies Jack externally while presenting his memories, perceptions, and emotional response.
The clipped fragment about an unidentified 'he' lacks enough context to establish the narrator's relationship to the story.
Generic aphoristic 'you' is not sustained address to a story protagonist.
A single sentence about an unidentified character's perception is compatible with either first- or third-person framing.
Impersonal scene description contains no diagnostic narrator-person evidence.
The isolated reference to 'he' does not by itself establish the controlling narrator's person.
Character speech does not identify the base narrator.
Sustained external narration names Sloat and Phil Sawyer while disclosing Sloat's retrospective thoughts.
Aphoristic commentary is not a diagnostic narrative scene.
The isolated third-person subject has insufficient local context to identify narrator participation.
Story-world exposition contains no person-marked narrator or sufficiently contextualized character reference.
Impersonal event description does not reveal the narrator's person.
Story-specific reflection may represent free-indirect thought, but its pronoun-free form does not independently identify narrator person.
The visible second-person forms occur entirely in character speech addressed to Jack.
Outside the dialogue, the narrator identifies Jack and Speedy externally and directly reports Jack's knowledge.
Two sentences sustain external access to an unidentified character's private difficulties, consistent with the book's third-person narration.
Generalizing statements about mortality are gnomic rather than diagnostic base narration.

The intrusive teller addresses the reader as 'you' and calls itself 'I' but remains outside the story, reporting the characters as 'they'; this is nonparticipating narration, not first-person participation.
First-person language appears only in a character's plea.
The isolated references to 'his father' do not establish whether the unshown narrator participates in the story.
The first-person wording is embedded graffiti; the surrounding frame is not independently diagnostic.

web_evidence.title: El Talismán — fragmento
web_evidence.note: Penguin's sustained authorized Spanish-language extract covers early chapters and consistently narrates Jack externally while entering his perceptions and thoughts.

web_evidence.title: The Talisman — publisher-formatted preview
web_evidence.note: The English preview supplies roughly the first seventy story pages, sustaining external Jack-focused narration and reporting his thoughts without a participating story narrator.

web_evidence.title: Stephen King Writing Styles in The Talisman
web_evidence.note: The study guide explicitly identifies an omniscient third-person narrative voice focused mainly on Jack, with occasional focal shifts to Morgan Sloat and Sunlight Gardener.

Opened and reviewed the Penguin authorized extract, the English publisher-formatted preview PDF, and the BookRags point-of-view discussion.
Checked Google Books metadata and contents, but its accessible page did not provide usable narrative prose; a Riverside Public Library excerpt returned an unsupported-content error when opened.
Located a scholarly thesis discussing focal shifts and an all-knowing narrator, but the repository PDF timed out or returned access denial, so it was not used as evidence.
person_note: The diagnostic quotes repeatedly show a nonparticipating narrator presenting Jack's and Sloat's actions, memories, and inner states. Two sustained authorized excerpts independently exhibit the same third-person pattern, and the whole-book point-of-view description explicitly confirms it while explaining the limited shifts among characters. The narratorial 'I' and reader-directed 'you' in q01029 are an intrusive outside teller's address, not participation as a story character; dialogue, gnomic 'you,' and graffiti are likewise local material. No evidence indicates sustained first- or second-person story sections. The remaining uncertainty is limited to the exact degree of omniscience, which does not affect the THIRD classification.
